title: Open Access Psychedelic Medicine Reviews!
subtitle: Now, there is no paywall between you and relatively well written reviews!
body_html:
Oh, dear readers. The things we do for academic publishing! The Frontier Psychiatrists is a daily-ish health-themed newsletter. It’s not listed on Google Scholar as a peer-reviewed journal. There is no peer review process beyond my very opinionated readers. Sometimes, this includes my wife. There is also more…comedy…in this writing, than would be typical in a science journal.

Share

However, one of the things this newsletter isn’t? A systematic review of all of the data on a given topic. That, it turns out, is a lot of work. If I am going to do that, it’s going to be published in a reputable journal. I’ve written about academic publishing and how scammy it can be previously.

Today, I have a present for my readers. I senior-authored a series of review articles on psychedelic medicines over the prior year, and they are systematic reviews of all the evidence to date. These were published in the American Journal of Theraputics, but I didn’t have the $20,000 plus dollars spare to make the 8-part series open access. Except, there was a cheat code! One of my coauthors had an academic affiliation with Oxford, which has a standing open-access contract with Lippincott, the publisher of the journal. So today, I am thrilled to present, for the first time, a series of academic papers on psychedelic medicines, now open-access —for the first time!

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Historical Perspective and Overview

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—3, 4-Methylenedioxy-methamphetamine (MDMA)

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Psilocybin

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Ibogaine

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Lysergic Acid Diethylamide (LSD)

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Ketamine

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—N, N-Dimethyltryptamine and Ayahuasca

Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—The Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats of Psychedelic Therapeutics

I hope you find these as helpful to read as I did to co-author. An extra special thank you to Burton Tabaac, M.D., and the invaluable Kenneth Shinozuka, BA, who did much of the first authoring of these papers and my other co-authors. Let it never be said I don’t write a lot.
